Article Title: Kentucky police officer Asad Zahir claimed he made 2048 Flock searches to track two vehicles for drug investigation. He was tracking his ex-girlfriend
Article Text:
Kentucky police officer Asad Zahir arrested and charged after he was found stalking his ex over 2000 times through Flock tracker.

It works, police department blames one officer's poor decisions

2048 Flock searches from January to May to track two vehicles

Another case of the misuse of Flock was reported after a Kentucky police officer was arrested for using the Flock Safety license plate reader camera system to track his ex-girlfriend, the mother of his child, 2000 time. Asad Zahir was arrested and then released on his own recognizance and will be presented in the court. Shively Police Department said that Zahir is suspended without pay pending the investigation.According to reports, Zahir's alleged activity was flagged by a new tool that Flock Safety brought in following the rise in the number of cases where the surveillance tool is being used to stalk exes. The audit assistance tool flags abnoram use by officers.“The Flock camera works. When it’s used properly it works. There are tons of stats that show it works,” Shively Police Chief Andre Bottoms said as Zahir's arrest was announced. “It’s a very effective tool and we don’t want to be judged on the poor decisions made by one officer.”Investigators found Zahir had conducted 2,048 Flock searches from January into May to track two vehicles registered to his ex in Kentucky and Indiana, court records show.During the period he conducted those searches, Zahir harassed the victim and made threatening comments, prompting her to file an order of protection against him, according to the court records.Investigators determined 241 Flock searches happened while that order of protection was in place, from April 17 to May 6, Bottoms said.Zahir has been an officer in the department since 2022. “Charging this officer was not pleasant. It was a gut punch for me personally,” Bottoms said, adding that he had come to personally know each member of the small police department. “Accountability cannot depend on who you are and what position you hold or what badge you’re wearing.”Zahir listed the reason for the Flock tracking as a drug or narcotics investigation, even though the woman who was targeted was not the subject of any such investigation and has no history indicating any such violations, officials said at the news conference.
Article Summary: Kentucky police officer Asad Zahir was arrested and charged after he was found stalking his ex over 2000 times through Flock tracker. Zahir listed the reason for the Flock tracking as a drug or narcotics investigation, even though the woman who was targeted was not the subject of any such investigation.

Article Title: A Houston lawyer bought a 15,000-sq-ft mansion listed for $15.5 million just to demolish it; he plans to donate about $4 million of its materials and turn the land into a garden
Article Text:
Houston attorney Tony Buzbee and his wife, Frances, recently acquired 1708 River Oaks Blvd

Salvaging luxury fixtures for charity

Property value and River Oaks history

A history of high-profile property moves

Creating a larger private garden

Prominent Houston trial lawyer Tony Buzbee has bought a 15,000-square-foot luxury mansion listed for $15.5 million in the exclusive River Oaks neighbourhood, with plans to tear down the entire house and turn the property into a private garden estate. The purchase of 1708 River Oaks Boulevard allows Buzbee and his wife, Frances Moody Buzbee, to expand their existing property directly beside their long-time home at 1722 River Oaks Boulevard. Instead of living in or renovating the large mansion, the couple has partnered with Habitat for Humanity to remove and save usable materials from the property before demolition begins.Reports from the Houston Business Journal and the Houston Chronicle confirmed that the non-profit will manage the salvage work, recovering millions of pounds of architectural fittings and building materials to support affordable housing projects across Texas. “They will be tearing it down and salvaging approximately $4 million worth of high-end materials, appliances, air units and the like for their mission,” Buzbee said in an email statement about the donation. “They are excited to have it, and we are proud to support them.”Under the agreement with Habitat for Humanity, salvage crews will carefully remove materials from inside and outside the 15,000-square-foot mansion before the site is cleared.The recovery work will include high-end kitchen equipment, custom woodwork, marble fittings, large air-conditioning units and other building materials. The donated materials are estimated to be worth $4 million. Habitat for Humanity plans to use some of the recovered items in affordable housing projects, while specialised fixtures may be sold through its ReStore shops to raise money for its work. Once the house is removed, the property will become a large private garden. The new green space will connect directly with the family’s main home next door, effectively doubling the size of their landscaped grounds along one of Houston’s best-known streets.The purchase reflects continued activity in River Oaks, an 1,100-acre master-planned community founded in 1924 by brothers Will and Mike Hogg and Hugh Potter. The neighbourhood remains one of Houston’s most exclusive residential areas and is controlled by strict deed restrictions and private maintenance rules overseen by the River Oaks Property Owners association. Harris Central Appraisal District records reviewed by Zillow show that 1708 River Oaks Boulevard had an assessed value of $18,062,181 in 2026. Official tax records show that the property had an annual tax bill of $383,861 before the sale. The $15.5 million asking price was therefore considerably below the official assessed value. Real estate publication The Real Deal said the purchase fits a growing trend known as landmaxxing. The term describes wealthy homeowners buying neighbouring properties, removing existing buildings and combining the lots into larger private estates.Buzbee, a former United States Marine Corps officer who ran for Houston mayor in 2019, has had a prominent presence on River Oaks Boulevard since buying his first home at 1722 River Oaks Boulevard for $14 million in 2013. In 2017, Buzbee drew widespread attention after buying a fully operational, demilitarised $600,000 World War II Sherman tank that had taken part in the Normandy landings. He parked the tank along the kerb outside his home, leading to a dispute with the local property owners association. He eventually donated the tank to Texas A&M University in 2018. The main estate also became the scene of a major police investigation in 2019 after burglars broke into the home following a Super Bowl event. They stole $21 million worth of artwork, jewellery, firearms and electronics. The items were later recovered after Buzbee offered a $50,000 reward for information that led to arrests. In February 2022, the couple put their 12,209-square-foot Tudor-style mansion on the market for $27.5 million through Douglas Elliman Real Estate. PaperCity Magazine and CultureMap Houston reported at the time that the listing even allowed buyers to pay in Bitcoin. When the home failed to sell at that price, the family decided to keep it and expand onto the neighbouring property instead.The demolition of 1708 River Oaks Boulevard will remove a mansion that included six bedrooms, an indoor swimming pool, a domed stained-glass ceiling, a lacquered library, a wine vault and a wellness wing with a beauty salon. Removing a fully functioning estate of this size is one of the more notable residential site clearances in recent Texas real estate. The work will happen in stages, starting with Habitat for Humanity’s salvage operation. Once workers have removed all usable fixtures and mechanical equipment, heavy machinery will bring down the remaining structure. Landscaping crews will then begin work on the garden extension. The finished project will join the two River Oaks lots into one large, connected green property. The expansion will give the family greater privacy while also sending millions of dollars worth of reusable construction materials towards charitable housing projects.
Article Summary: Houston attorney Tony Buzbee and his wife, Frances, recently acquired 1708 River Oaks Blvd. The couple has partnered with Habitat for Humanity to remove and save usable materials from the property before demolition begins. The recovery work will include high-end kitchen equipment, custom woodwork, marble fittings, large air-conditioning units and other building materials. The donated materials are estimated to be worth $4 million.

Article Title: Last known location-Hotel Kailash: NRI couple from Canada Dhaval Shah, Megha missing in Nepal
Article Text:
NRI couple Dhaval Shah, Megha Shah went missing in Nepal.

British Columbia couple Dhaval Shah, Megha Shah missing in Nepal.

Statement from tour operator

Family members of Dhaval Shah and Megha Shah circulated a missing poster in and around British Columbia, hoping to get some information about the duo who went on a tour in the Timure region which is believed to be completely wiped out in the devastating flood. Dhaval's cousin Nikita Shah told Global News that Dhaval and Megha were last known to be at Hotel Kailash.Megha Shah, 50, and her husband, Dhaval Shah, 52, are among 30 Canadians and permanent residents listed as missing by Global Affairs Canada after the disaster. Shubhakshi (Shubhi) Rawla and Sumit Rawla, both 50, have also not been heard from since the flood, with their last reported sighting at a tea stall in Timure, where they were staying at the Hotel Kailash.The Shahs and the Rawlas were traveling with a group of 47 people, including 10 Canadians on a pilgrimage around the base of Mount Kailash in Tibet organized by Himalayan Glacier Adventures.Dhaval's brother Keval Shah, who is in Mumbai, told Vancouver Sun that the Shahs left for the two-week trek on August 24 and he last spoke with him Sunday. "He was going to come and meet me after in Mumbai on Sept. 7," Keval said.The Shah couple have a daughter who stayed home during the trip.Dhaval has lived in Canada for about two decades and works as a cargo ship captain. Nikita said she hoped that since Dhaval works in the Navy, he was able to use some of his training to save himself and his wife.“So the Hotel Kailash, from what we understand, is like about 1.5 km from the checkpoint, so they were somewhere in that location and, you know, the (tour) company lost contact with anybody at around 8:30 that morning, so we don’t know where they have been since then," Nikita said.“Of course, there’s images that we see, but then there’s also all this information that we get that they could be at a higher elevation, they could be there, they could have run.”Himalayan Glacier Adventures said in a social media statement Wednesday that communication with the group was “extremely difficult” after the floods damaged mobile and electrical infrastructure. “We completely understand how worrying and distressing this uncertainty must be for you and your family, especially with concern surrounding the Kailash Yatra pilgrims who were travelling through the affected region,” the company said in the statement.
Article Summary: Dhaval Shah, 52, and Megha Shah, 50, are among 30 Canadians and permanent residents listed as missing by Global Affairs Canada. The Shahs and the Rawlas were traveling with a group of 47 people, including 10 Canadians on a pilgrimage around the base of Mount Kailash in Tibet.

Article Title: In 2024, a Colorado county paid $34 million for a 650-acre ranch privately owned for more than a century; 2 years later, 530 acres are being transferred into the Maroon Bells-Snowmass Wilderness
Article Text:
In 2024, a Colorado county paid $34 million for a 650-acre ranch privately owned for more than a century

A century of private ownership

Financing the record purchase

Protecting important wildlife habitat

In a major expansion of protected public land, 530 acres of a historic Colorado mountain ranch are being formally added to the Maroon Bells-Snowmass Wilderness, two years after local officials secured the property in a record $34 million purchase. Known as Snowmass Falls Ranch, the 650-acre property sits in the upper Snowmass Creek Valley and had been privately owned for more than a century. Pitkin County bought the property in 2024 through its Open Space and Trails programme to prevent it from being divided for housing. Under the planned agreement, most of the ranch will be transferred to the United States Forest Service and permanently added to the surrounding 181,535-acre federal wilderness area. The transfer completes a decades-long effort by conservationists to protect the environmentally sensitive valley floor, which lies at the foot of the Elk Mountains.Before European settlement, the land was part of the historic territory of the Ute People. In the early 20th century, Danish immigrant Kate Lindvig put together several parcels through the Homestead Act and direct purchases. She became known as the "Cattle Queen of Snow Mass".Lindvig ran the ranch on her own until 1943, when she sold it to Bob Perry, his wife Ruth Brown Perry and her brother, D.R.C. Brown, Jr. The Perry family looked after the property for nearly 80 years before eventually putting it on the market. The ranch was listed for sale in 2021 for $50 million. With property prices rising rapidly in Pitkin County, local conservation groups feared that the rare, connected stretch of land could be divided into expensive luxury homes. “Snowmass Falls Ranch is quite easily the most extraordinary piece of private land in Pitkin County,” said Dale Will, acquisition and projects director for Pitkin County Open Space and Trails, during public discussions about the proposal. “We've held our breath since the property was listed, but never gave up on the hope that the ranch could be preserved”.The $34 million purchase was the largest open space acquisition in Pitkin County’s history, doubling the previous record of $17 million paid for Sky Mountain Park in 2010. The county financed the deal through open space bonds issued in 2020, along with a $10 million loan from Great Outdoors Colorado (GOCO). The organisation distributes state lottery money to support conservation projects by local governments. Additional help came from The Wilderness Land Trust, which worked with local officials on the federal land transfer process. According to local news outlet The Slope, official records published through Pitkin County’s civic alert portal and financial information from Alpine Bank, the deal was designed to allow the county to sell a large part of the ranch to the federal government later. The county plans to transfer 530 acres into the White River National Forest using money from the Land and Water Conservation Fund (LWCF). This will allow Pitkin County to recover a significant part of the money it spent buying the property. The remaining 120 acres contain historic farm buildings and basic cabins. These will remain under county control or be protected through a conservation easement to preserve the land and maintain future public access.The ranch is surrounded on three sides by federally protected wilderness and contains a range of habitats, including beaver ponds, spruce forests, alpine wetlands and large aspen groves. The property also has two miles of frontage along Snowmass Creek and holds senior water rights that are important for agricultural and municipal supplies downstream. The land provides important summer habitat for native wildlife, including elk, mule deer, moose, black bears and mountain lions. It also contains two natural waterfalls, including Snowmass Falls, which gives the ranch its name. The property is also important for outdoor recreation. Two major U.S. Forest Service trails cross the ranch, giving hikers and backpackers routes into the Maroon Bells-Snowmass area. With the land now under county ownership and being transferred to federal protection, public access to the trailheads will be secured permanently, ending long-running access concerns near the entrance. Gary Tennenbaum, director of Pitkin County Open Space and Trails, described the acquisition as an important moment for conservation in the county during the early stages of the purchase. “The final pieces of major public land in Pitkin County that we haven't been able to conserve are out there, and this was one of them, and it was a big one,” Tennenbaum noted. “We hope to transfer most of the ranch to the Forest Service as soon as possible, but for now, this amazing property will be open space”. With 530 acres now moving into federal management, the former private property will receive permanent protection under the Wilderness Act. The move ensures that the upper valley floor will remain undeveloped and open to the public for generations to come.
Article Summary: Pitkin County bought Snowmass Falls Ranch in 2024 for $34 million. The 650-acre property has been privately owned for more than a century. Most of the ranch will be transferred to the United States Forest Service. The remaining 120 acres contain historic farm buildings and basic cabins. The land provides important summer habitat for native wildlife.

Article Title: Flock CEO Garrett Langley's address leaked online after he urged Americans to 'compromise' between privacy and safety
Article Text:
Flock CEO's address was leaked online after he urged Americans to choose a compromise between privacy and safety.

What is the controversy over Flock cameras?

Senator launches investigation into Flock

Flock CEO Garrett Langley emerged as the most controversial personality of this month as his surveillance technology company is facing massive backlash because of the huge scope of misuse of the technology. It is not confirmed whether the address shared online is Langley's real address. Many social media users shared a screenshot of a blurred Google map and claimed that Langley got his house blurred on Google map while asking Americans to compromise on privacy.Flock, according to the company, is designed to help authorized users find relevant evidence for investigations without compromising safety and compliance. Flock cameras can read license plates and they can record and analyze everything that passes them.But instances of misusing this technology are plenty. A Kentucky police officer was arrested after authorities said he used the Flock Safety license plate reader camera system to track his ex-girlfriend over 2,000 times.Protesters vandalized these traffic cameras as people are waking up to the threat of the new tech and some cities have canceled their Flock contracts.Langley acknowledged the initial loopholes and said they were working on it, but Americans must compromise on their compromise when it is a question of safety, he said. “When people talk about just one of these, privacy or safety, they’re prioritizing the wrong thing, and what we have to prioritize as a country is compromise,” Langley said in the interview. “How do we have our safety, and how do we balance privacy?”"I value my privacy. My family values their privacy. My employees value their privacy. But what we are talking about is safety as well," he said adding that cars have never been banned because they cause accidents.Sen. Josh Hawley (R-Mo.), the chair of the Senate Judiciary Subcommittee on Crime and Counterterrorism, has launched an investigation into Flock Safety’s national surveillance network and is demanding to know who has access to the personal data of Americans captured on Flock cameras. “The overwhelming majority of Americans captured in those records did nothing wrong. Instead of serving discrete local investigations, as contemplated by our constitutional processes and safeguards, these camera networks harness artificial intelligence to pool what they capture into a national database that customers can search,” Hawley wrote in a letter to Flock CEO.
Article Summary: Flock CEO Garrett Langley's address was leaked online after he urged Americans to choose a compromise between privacy and safety. Many social media users shared a screenshot of a blurred Google map and claimed that Langley got his house blurred on Google map while asking Americans to compromise on privacy. Senator Josh Hawley (R-Mo.) has launched an investigation into Flock Safety’s national surveillance network.

Article Title: A Texas farmer’s family has worked 6,000 acres for over a century; after his landlord sold 600 rented acres for a Google data center, he was given 60 days to leave
Article Text:
Corporate expansion across rural Texas

Growing pressure on farmland

Huge projects, huge energy needs

Standing near the Haskell County border in West Texas, fourth-generation farmer Cheyenne Buerger can see industrial cranes building a huge Google facility just over four miles to the northeast. Until recently, part of that same horizon was farmland he worked himself. After farming thousands of acres with his family for more than a century, Buerger was forced to give up 600 acres of rented farmland when his landlord suddenly sold the property to a developer clearing the site for the tech giant. The eviction gave the local farmer very little time to harvest his remaining crops and leave the land. "When I explained I had a crop on it, they said 'You can finish it, but that's it,'" Buerger said. "'You've got to be done in 60 days, and you're out." Losing the land near Haskell has taken away a large part of Buerger's local farming operation. Along with his family's 6,000 acres, where they grow cotton, wheat and milo, the rented fields gave the family more flexibility for crop rotations and livestock management. "It makes me feel a little threatened just from losing land to data centers," Buerger said. "We can't compete with that."The loss of farmland to technology projects is becoming more common across Texas, according to an investigation by The Texas Tribune. As major technology companies expand artificial intelligence and cloud computing, developers are moving into rural counties looking for large, flat and relatively cheap areas of land. Data from the Pew Research Center shows that about 67 per cent of data centres in the United States are located in rural areas. In Texas, low taxes and large amounts of available land have long attracted major industries, but the current growth of data centres has reached new levels. An analysis by The Texas Tribune found 335 operating data centres across Texas, with at least 248 more either planned or under construction. The fast conversion of farmland into large server campuses is causing concern among farmers who are increasingly competing with wealthy technology companies for land and other important resources, including groundwater and electricity.The expansion comes at a difficult time for Texas agriculture. The industry produces more than $963 billion in total economic activity and generates nearly $15 billion in annual exports, according to state production figures cited in the report. State officials have also criticised the choice of farmland for some of these projects. Speaking at a public forum on rural industrial development organised by The Texas Tribune in Granbury, Texas Agriculture Commissioner Sid Miller warned that turning fertile soil into technology sites could permanently reduce the state's ability to produce food. "They're building them on our most valuable, most fertile farmland," said Texas Agriculture Commissioner Sid Miller. "Once our farmland is gone and paved over, we'll never farm it again." The amount of land needed for some of these projects is enormous. Three major developments, Project Matador in the Panhandle, Project Pacifico in Pecos County and Project Meta in El Paso, are expected to cover at least 16,000 acres combined. That is roughly equal to 12,000 American football fields.In Hereford, about 50 miles southwest of Amarillo, Google outlined plans for its multi-phase Project Roman during a public community meeting. Local farmer Darren Grotegut attended the meeting and learned that the first phase alone would use 3,700 acres for computing facilities. More land would be needed for solar and wind projects to provide electricity. Grotegut estimated that all four phases could eventually cover more than 180,000 acres. To reduce the large amount of water needed to cool the computer equipment, project representatives said some nearby farmland could be converted into native grasslands to help protect local aquifers. The pressure on rural land is not limited to data centres. Clean energy monitoring company Cleanview says 240 utility-scale solar farms are now operating on rural Texas land. By 2024, about 1.5 million acres of former farmland across the state had been converted to solar energy production. For farmers such as Buerger, the future of tenant farming in West Texas looks increasingly uncertain. He still hauls cotton seed across his remaining pastures to feed cattle while construction crews put up steel frames on the fields he once rented. As investors and energy developers continue buying large connected areas of land across Jones and Haskell counties, family farmers have fewer options for finding replacement acreage. Rising land prices linked to industrial development are also making it harder for them to compete. Across the region, farming communities are facing lasting changes in how land, water and electricity are used.
Article Summary: Technology companies are moving into rural counties looking for large, flat and relatively cheap areas of land. An analysis by The Texas Tribune found 335 operating data centres across Texas, with at least 248 more either planned or under construction. By 2024, about 1.5 million acres of former farmland across the state had been converted to solar energy production.

Article Title: 'Engine issue at 31,000 feet': New Jersey-bound United Airlines flight makes emergency landing in Nevada
Article Text:
United Airlines flight makes emergeny landing in Las Vegas, Nevada.

United Airlines transcontinental flight makes emergency landing in London

A New Jersey-bound United Airlines flight made an emergency landing in Nevada Thursday after reporting an engine issue. United Airlines flight 1403 departed Los Angeles before landing safely at Las Vegas’ Harry Reid International Airport around 7 am after encountering a problem with one of the aircraft’s engines, according to the Federal Aviation Administration and United Airlines.The 176 passengers and seven crew members deplaned after the engine snafu and are awaiting another flight to their destination at Newark Liberty International Airport, an airline spokesperson told The New York Post.“United Flight 1403 LA to NY… engine failure at 31,000 feet! Emergency landing at Las Vegas Airport. Terrifying!” one user wrote on X, alongside a picture of a passenger window of the Boeing 757.Authorities have not confirmed what kind of engine issue forced the emergency landing.The Newark incident comes close on the heels of a similar incident of the same airline but on a transcontinental flight earlier this week. A United Airlines flight heading to New Jersey from Rome had to make an emergency landing in London following mid-flight technical issues. Flight UA169 departed Venice Marco Polo Airport on Monday morning for Newark with 216 passengers. But after an hour, the plane approached Heathrow.It had to circle the London airport to get rid of excess fuel ahead of the unscheduled landing.The United Airlines flight eventually landed at Heathrow without issues about two and a half hours after departing Venice. The airline has not disclosed what mechanical issue affected the flight. It is also unclear when the passengers were rebooked onto another flight to continue their journey to Newark. “United flight 169 from Venice to Newark diverted to London Heathrow to address a mechanical issue. The aircraft landed safely, and we are working to rebook customers on the next available flight to EWR,” a spokesperson said.
Article Summary: United Airlines flight 1403 departed Los Angeles before landing safely at Las Vegas’ Harry Reid International Airport around 7 am. The 176 passengers and seven crew members deplaned after the engine snafu and are awaiting another flight to their destination at Newark Liberty International Airport.

Article Title: Hindu priest arrested in Canada for sexually assaulting woman under guise of healing
Article Text:
Rajendranauth Doodnauth MARAJ,/Image: Durham Regional Police

A US-based Hindu priest has been arrested in Oshawa, Canada, for sexually assaulting a woman under the guise of a religious healing ceremony.Police said the victim and her family had hired the priest, identified as Rajendranauth Doodnauth Maraj, 50, to travel from the US to perform a Hindu religious ceremony. Maraj is from Richmond Hill, New York.According to Durham Regional Police, Maraj told the woman that she was possessed by evil spirits and convinced her that she needed a specific ceremony to be healed. Police said he then exploited her trust in his religious role and brought her to a private location, where he allegedly sexually assaulted her while claiming to be carrying out the ceremony.Officers from the East Division responded to a sexual assault call on Tuesday, August 25, in the area of Harmony Road North and Conlin Road East. Maraj was later taken into custody .He has been charged with one count of sexual assault and was held for a bail hearing.
Article Summary: Rajendranauth Doodnauth Maraj, 50, is from Richmond Hill, New York. He told the woman that she was possessed by evil spirits and convinced her that she needed a specific ceremony to be healed. Police said he exploited her trust in his religious role and brought her to a private location.

Article Title: US college student shot dead by police after knocking on wrong house amid burglary call
Article Text:
22-year-old college student was shot and killed by police in Pennsylvania. (AP Photo)

A 22-year-old college student was shot and killed by police in Pennsylvania after he mistakenly went to the wrong house and was waiting for his friends to pick him up, his father said.Police in Upper Pottsgrove Township, northwest of Philadelphia, responded around 12:30 am Sunday to a 911 call reporting a possible break-in, CNN reported citing Montgomery County district attorney’s office. Officers found Glenwood Pysher IV at the rear of the house and later shot him dead.Pysher’s father, Glen Pysher, said his son had been out with friends at several bars before they split up to spend the night at two different homes.According to what his son’s friends told him, Pysher took a wrong turn through the woods and mistakenly went to a house he believed belonged to a friend.Pysher was carrying only his phone and a backpack with clothes and a few beers, his father said. He allegedly tried to open the door and called out, “Hey! Open the door!” believing he was at his friend’s home.After realising the mistake, Pysher sat on the back porch and contacted his friends.They then started heading to the house to pick him up.His friends later saw police and emergency vehicles at the location and initially believed Pysher would be arrested for public drunkenness. Instead, he had been shot.Pysher’s father said his son was on a FaceTime call with his friends at 12:32 am, while police were dispatched at 12:30 am and arrived at 12:34 am, according to a Montgomery County Department of Public Safety dispatch record.The father questioned what happened during the brief interval before his son was shot.Upper Pottsgrove Township Police Chief Al Werner has declined to release details, including the names of the officers involved, pending the investigation.The Montgomery County Detective Bureau is investigating the shooting, the district attorney’s office said.Pysher was due to begin his senior year at Saint Elizabeth University in New Jersey, where he planned to play baseball. He hoped to become a high school history teacher and coach after graduating.His father described him as kind-hearted and loving, saying former teammates, coaches and others had reached out with memories of him since his death.The family has also said it has received little information from police.Pysher’s father said he was recently told he could collect his son’s favourite black shoes so they could be used for his burial, but was later told officials needed to consider whether they could release them.
Article Summary: Police in Upper Pottsgrove Township, northwest of Philadelphia, responded around 12:30 am Sunday to a 911 call reporting a possible break-in. Officers found Glenwood Pysher IV at the rear of the house and later shot him dead. He had been out with friends at several bars before they split up to spend the night at two different homes.

Article Title: 'It's your sense of entitlement': US officials slam Indian-origin entrepreneur Ankit Gupta over H-1B comments
Article Text:
Indian-origin serial entrepreneur Ankit Gupta, general partner of YC, is at the center of a major social media storm over his comments on H-1B which he deleted later.

Who is Ankit Gupta ? What is the latest H-1B controversy?

Ankit Gupta was accused of deriding Americans as he was defending the H-1B immigrant culture.

White House official reacts, YC CEO issues statement

Indian-American entrepreneur Ankit Gupta landed in a soup after his H-1B comments on social media that stirred the hornet's nest, following which Gupta made his X account private. Inspector General of the US Department of Labor took note of Gupta's comment and slammed him publicly, calling out what he termed as his "sense of entitlement". Chairman of the Federal Trade Commission of the United States Andrew Ferguson said individuals like Gupta do not have the best interests of Americans in their minds.Gupta, a distinguished computer scientist from Harvard, is a serial entrepreneur and currently a partner of Y Combinator. Before joining YC, he was the co-founder and CTO of Reveries Labs. The controversy that he landed in stemmed from his comment on JD Vance's post."If an American corporation needs workers, it should hire and train Americans," Vice President JD Vance wrote on X, reacting to the Donald Trump administration's new H-1B visa fee. "in a win for the woke left DEI is back," Ankit Gupta commented, suggesting that if Americans have to be hired because they are Americans and not because of their skill, then it is DEI (Diversity, Equity and Inlcusion) only.The now-deleted post and the sarcasm did not go down well with America First commentators, and then it came to the notice of the DOL's Inspector General."Ankit Gupta thinks hiring Americans first—in America—is “DEI.” No, Ankit. It’s called putting your own citizens first. American companies. American jobs. American workers first. If that offends you, the problem isn’t America. It’s your sense of entitlement," D'Esposito said.As Gupta defended the H-1B hiring by Silicon Valley, he asked one commentator: 'what elements of H-1B immigrant culture do you not like? is it the willingness to work long hours? Or perhaps the education focus of their children?""Leaving trash everywhere, scamming people, endemic pathological dishonesty, atrocious aesthetic taste, need I go on," the commentator replied. "It's giving flyover country," Gupta wrote. Social media users started flagging this comment as a racist attack aimed at rural white Americans and asked YC to take action against Gupta."Hey @ycombinator this is a racist attack aimed at rural White Americans. Your policies mention that you do not tolerate any racism. It states that racial discrimination is a fireable offense. When can we expect you to fire Ankit Gupta?" one wrote.Chairman of the Federal Trade Commission of the United States Andrew Ferguson, responded to the controversy and called YCombinator "a front for the far left"."Y Combinator is a supposed champion of “Little Tech” but perhaps they’re nothing more than a front for the far left. I’m deeply uncomfortable with wealthy investors attacking American workers like this. I’m afraid it’s increasingly obvious to many people that individuals such as this guy do not have the best interests of America and her citizens in mind," Ferguson wrote, referring to Gupta."The purpose of the American economy is to promote the general welfare of American workers, not provide jobs for the rest of the world," he said.Y Combinator president and CEO Garry Tan issued a statement saying that YC supports hiring and funding Americans.
Article Summary: Indian-American entrepreneur Ankit Gupta landed in a soup after his H-1B comments on social media that stirred the hornet's nest. Inspector General of the US Department of Labor took note of Gupta's comment and slammed him publicly, calling out what he termed as his "sense of entitlement" Chairman of the Federal Trade Commission of the United States Andrew Ferguson said individuals like Gupta do not have the best interests of Americans in their minds.

Article Title: RSS chief Mohan Bhagwat's US event organiser AHEAD’s X account restored after brief suspension
Article Text:
The X account of RSS chief Mohan Bhagwat’s US event organiser, which was suspended, has now been restored.

The X (formerly Twitter) account of American Hindus for Engagement and Dialogue (AHEAD), which is organising Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh ( RSS ) chief Mohan Bhagwat ’s event at New York’s Madison Square Garden, has been restored after a brief suspension. AHEAD said it believes opponents used automated activity to get the account blocked and thanked X for restoring it.“We are back up! We got ‘botted’ by misguided opponents who tried to game the X algorithm and get our handle blocked. A big thank you to @X @Support for the prompt response, restoring our account and clearing out the bots. Now, back to what really matters: celebrating Universal Harmony and Universal Oneness @Uni1ness,” AHEAD said in a post on X.The account, operating under the handle @AheadForum1, had earlier become unavailable to users on Thursday. AHEAD had initially said it believed the suspension may have occurred in error.Bhagwat is scheduled to address the “Universal Oneness Celebration” at the Infosys Theatre at Madison Square Garden on August 29. The programme is expected to draw around 5,000 Indian Americans as part of the RSS's global outreach during its centenary yearEarlier this week, New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani said he did not support the planned event, while acknowledging that his office may not have the authority to cancel a private gathering.“I don’t support the rally, but I don’t know if the city has any jurisdiction on cancelling a private event,” Mamdani told reporters on Tuesday.Mamdani's comments have triggered criticism among sections of the Indian-American diaspora and have also drawn opposing reactions from Indian political parties. His remarks came as left-liberal groups criticised the event and called for its cancellation.The controversy has also prompted a security advisory from the Hindu American Foundation (HAF), a US-based non-profit organisation. HAF urged people attending the event to remain vigilant, stay aware of their surroundings and keep interactions civil.HAF said the advisory followed attempts by activists targeting Hindu Americans to disrupt and cancel the celebration.It also called on Mamdani to ensure the safety of people attending the event.The event has also drawn scrutiny from the United States Commission on International Religious Freedom (USCIRF), which has urged the US government to consider sanctions against RSS members and Indian officials it alleges are involved in religious freedom violations in India.“We urge the US government to consider targeted sanctions against RSS members and Indian officials complicit in religious freedom violations, including revoking the visa issued to Mohan Bhagwat and making him ineligible for future entry into the United States,” the body said.The commission is chaired by Pakistani-American Asif Mahmood.India's Ministry of External Affairs has previously rejected USCIRF's assessments, accusing the body of bias and questioning its credibility. During an August 21 press briefing, MEA spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal said the commission had made what he described as “incorrect and provocative statements about India” for years.“We all know this is a biased institution. For years, it has made incorrect and provocative statements about India. We should ignore such institutions, as they have their own agendas and lack credibility,” Jaiswal said.
Article Summary: The X (formerly Twitter) account of American Hindus for Engagement and Dialogue (AHEAD) has been restored after a brief suspension. AHEAD is organising Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh ( RSS ) chief Mohan Bhagwat ’s event at New York’s Madison Square Garden. The account, operating under the handle @AheadForum1, had earlier become unavailable to users.

Article Title: US man steals fire truck from crews battling his burning home in New Hampshire, crashes it
Article Text:
30-year-old Nestor Roman II of Dalton.

A New Hampshire man allegedly stole a rescue truck from firefighters battling a blaze at his own home, drove over active fire hoses and crashed into a fire engine before fleeing the scene, authorities said.According to the New York Post, 30-year-old Nestor Roman II of Dalton faces multiple felony and misdemeanor charges over the early-morning incident on August 25. The fire broke out near Faraway Road and Mountain Road, with several nearby departments responding to assist Dalton Fire & Rescue.New Hampshire State Police said troopers were heading to the scene around 3:50 am when they learned that a Whitefield Fire & Rescue vehicle had been stolen.Roman allegedly got behind the wheel of an F550 rescue truck shortly before 5 am while firefighters were still fighting the blaze.Officials said Roman drove around a Whitefield fire engine, nearly hitting two firefighters and narrowly missing a third who could have been trapped between the vehicles. He then allegedly crashed the stolen truck into the fire engine and a pickup.The rescue truck also ran over multiple water-supply lines, including two charged hoses being used to battle the fire.The hoses were not damaged, officials said.Roman allegedly continued driving, striking a firefighter's personal vehicle and damaging wooden fences at two nearby properties before fleeing.The chase ended several miles away after a Dalton homeowner reported that the stolen rescue vehicle had crashed on their property. The homeowner also told police that the driver was allegedly trying to take items from the porch.Troopers found Roman there and took him into custody after he was initially uncooperative, police said.Roman faces three felony counts of reckless conduct with a deadly weapon, burglary and two counts of theft by unauthorized taking. He also faces several misdemeanor charges, including conduct after an accident, obstructing government administration, resisting arrest, driving after suspension and driving over a fire hose without consent.Despite significant damage, the Whitefield fire engine remained operational and firefighters eventually extinguished the blaze.Officials said the house was a "complete loss."The New Hampshire State Fire Marshal's Office is investigating the cause of the fire. No firefighters were physically injured in the incident, Dalton Fire & Rescue said.
Article Summary: Nestor Roman II, 30, faces multiple felony and misdemeanor charges over the early-morning incident on August 25. The fire broke out near Faraway Road and Mountain Road, with several nearby departments responding to assist Dalton Fire & Rescue.Roman allegedly got behind the wheel of an F550 rescue truck shortly before 5 am while firefighters were still fighting the blaze.

Article Title: Trump admin restricts foreign student internships, warns universities could lose certification over CPT violations
Article Text:
Trump admin restricts foreign student internships.

The Trump administration has warned US universities that they could lose certification to enrol international students if they fail to comply with federal rules governing Curricular Practical Training (CPT) work authorisations.A memo issued on August 24 by the Student and Exchange Visitor Program, part of US Immigration and Customs Enforcement, said the agency had identified an increase in CPT authorisations that appeared to violate federal requirements, according to Reuters.CPT allows eligible international students to undertake internships or other practical training when the work is an integral part of their academic curriculum.The memo said the training must be connected to an established course of study.“Failure to comply with SEVP regulations may result in an institution losing certification to enrol foreign students,” it said.The guidance has prompted some universities to suspend or review certain internship applications for international students.The University of California, Los Angeles said it had paused some CPT authorisations while examining the federal directive.“UCLA has paused certain Curricular Practical Training authorizations while it reviews recent federal guidance and determines next steps,” a university spokesperson said.The University of California, Berkeley said the August 24 memo was narrower and more direct than an earlier directive issued in mid-August, but included stricter requirements.Its international office said it was unlikely to process some internship work authorisation applications “in the near future” and advised affected students to plan accordingly.The university said it would continue processing CPT applications linked to degree requirements. It also said it would resume processing CPT applications for doctoral dissertation and master’s thesis research and consult legal experts on procedures to meet the new requirements.The Department of Homeland Security, which oversees ICE, said the underlying regulations had not changed.“Nothing about these regulations has changed,” the department said. “However, schools and employers should consider themselves on notice: under President Trump, abuse of this generous system will no longer be tolerated.”The warning is part of a broader campaign by the Trump administration targeting US universities. Federal agencies have opened investigations and threatened funding over issues including pro-Palestinian protests, diversity programmes, climate initiatives and transgender policies.The administration has also revoked visas held by some foreign students involved in pro-Palestinian protests. Officials have described some demonstrations as antisemitic or supportive of extremist groups.Protesters, including Jewish organisations, have rejected that description. They say criticism of Israel’s military campaign in Gaza and its occupation of Palestinian territories is not antisemitic and that support for Palestinian rights does not amount to support for extremism.The Justice Department has separately expanded its scrutiny of university admissions. On Thursday, it alleged that admissions practices at George Washington University School of Medicine and Health Sciences favoured Black and Hispanic applicants.The university disputed the findings.“We are disappointed by the DOJ’s conclusions, which we believe are incorrect,” it said, adding that its admissions policies complied with the law and were not discriminatory.The Justice Department has made similar allegations against other universities and said it was seeking settlement talks. It has threatened to file lawsuits if those discussions fail.
Article Summary: US universities warned they could lose certification to enrol international students if they fail to comply with federal rules governing Curricular Practical Training (CPT) work authorisations. CPT allows eligible international students to undertake internships or other practical training when the work is an integral part of their academic curriculum.

Article Title: In 1856, one of Northern California’s oldest cattle ranches was established; 170 years later, its 14,177 acres are being bought for $15.5 million and opened to the public
Article Text:
In 1856, one of Northern California’s oldest cattle ranches was established

Protecting headwaters and wildlife corridors

From working ranch to public preserve

The Wildlands Conservancy has agreed to buy one of Northern California’s oldest working livestock operations, protecting 14,177 acres of historic wilderness in Siskiyou County and turning it into a huge public preserve. The $15.5 million purchase of the AP Ranch, detailed in reports by the San Francisco Chronicle and official documents from The Wildlands Conservancy, marks a major change for a landscape that has been privately owned for 170 years. Located in rural western Siskiyou County near Gazelle, the vast property will be combined with the existing 6,094-acre Beaver Valley Headwaters Preserve. Once the deal is complete, the connected public preserve will cover more than 20,000 acres across the Scott River watershed. Founded in 1856 by Alexander Parker soon after the California Gold Rush, the AP Ranch is one of the region’s oldest continuously operating agricultural properties. The Newton family bought the estate in 1961 and later expanded it by purchasing nearby land. They ran the property as a year-round cow-calf operation with capacity for about 500 mother cows. According to listing details from California Outdoor Properties, the ranch has varied terrain centred around the prominent Lover’s Leap peak.Elevations range from about 3,600 feet to 5,400 feet, with the Marble Mountain Wilderness and Klamath National Forest forming the backdrop.The purchase is important not only because of the ranch’s history, but also because of its ecological value. The AP Ranch contains the headwaters of the East Fork of the Scott River, which runs freely for eight miles through the property. The Scott River provides important spawning habitat for wild Coho salmon, king salmon and steelhead trout. The deal also includes extensive adjudicated water rights on the East Fork and its tributaries, as well as rights connected to two alpine lakes, Kangaroo Lake and Rock Fence Lake. Conservationists hope these rights will help protect water flows during the dry summer months, when falling water levels can make it harder for migratory fish to survive and move through the watershed. The Wildlands Conservancy said the surrounding landscape is also an important link for wildlife moving through mixed-conifer forests, oak woodlands and alpine meadows. The expanded preserve will border thousands of acres of federal forest land and provide habitat for many native species, including Roosevelt elk, Columbia blacktail deer, black bears, mountain lions, wild turkeys and American goshawks. The area is also within the growing range of California’s recovering gray wolf packs. Rewilding work will focus on restoring habitats and supporting native wildlife. The Scott River basin is home to American beavers, a keystone species whose dams can slow water, restore floodplains and help recharge groundwater. The conservancy plans to work with local tribal and environmental groups, including the Quartz Valley Indian Reservation, the Karuk Tribe, the Lomakatsi Restoration Project, California Trout and the Scott River Watershed Council, to improve the health of the wider watershed.The sale brings an end to more than six decades of ownership by the Newton family. Albert Newton III said the family had developed a deep personal connection to the land during its long tenure. “Over the years, the ranch has hosted everyone from dignitaries and politicians to our kids' college friends,” Newton said, highlighting the property’s role as a gathering place in the Scott Valley. The AP Ranch includes seven homes, six historic timber barns and large cattle corrals equipped with certified scales. Under the new plan, The Wildlands Conservancy will gradually end intensive commercial operations while developing facilities for public use. The non-profit organisation operates California’s largest private preserve system and welcomes more than 1.5 million visitors each year to protected areas across California and Utah, with no admission fee. The new preserve will offer free public access for activities such as hiking, wildlife watching and educational trips for local schools. Higher parts of the property have views towards Mount Shasta and will also offer opportunities for winter activities, including cross-country skiing and snowshoeing. Fundraising is now underway. The Wildlands Conservancy is seeking private donations and public grants to cover the $15.5 million purchase and support long-term management, trail building and habitat restoration across the newly protected landscape.
Article Summary: The $15.5 million purchase of the AP Ranch marks a major change for a landscape that has been privately owned for 170 years. Located in rural western Siskiyou County, the vast property will be combined with the existing 6,094-acre Beaver Valley Headwaters Preserve. Once the deal is complete, the connected public preserve will cover more than 20,000 acres.

Article Title: US judge blocks Trump admin's Anthropic sanctions, calls them unlawful
Article Text:
President Donald Trump listens as Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth speaks at a cabinet meeting. (AP Photo)

Anthropic welcomed ruling

Anthropic faces separate Pentagon action

A US federal judge has ruled that the Trump administration acted unlawfully in targeting AI firm Anthropic after it resisted certain military uses of its models, saying national security cannot be used to justify retaliation against government critics.US District Judge Rita Lin said the government’s decision to designate Anthropic as a “supply chain risk” was unlawful and violated the company’s constitutional rights, according to the BBC.“The empty invocation of national security is not a blank check to punish and retaliate against government critics,” Lin said in her 59-page ruling.The ruling blocks federal agencies named in Anthropic’s lawsuit from enforcing President Donald Trump’s directive restricting the use of the company’s Claude AI tools.It also overturns former Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth’s decision to classify Anthropic as a supply-chain risk — a designation generally used against companies linked to countries considered security threats.The decision makes permanent an earlier temporary suspension of the sanctions and takes effect immediately. The administration can challenge the ruling before a higher court.Anthropic welcomed the court decision, saying it remained committed to working with the US government on national security applications of AI.“We welcome the court’s ruling that this supply chain risk designation was unlawful,” an Anthropic spokesperson said, according to the BBC.The dispute began after Anthropic refused to allow its AI models to be used for fully autonomous lethal weapons and mass surveillance of Americans.The company argued that its models were not sufficiently reliable for safe deployment in weapons systems and that domestic surveillance could violate constitutional rights.Trump had sharply criticised Anthropic, describing it as a “radical left, woke company” and accusing it of trying to control military activity through its terms of service.Lin said the government's actions appeared to be aimed at punishing Anthropic for challenging the administration rather than addressing a genuine national security threat.In an earlier stage of the case, she had said the government appeared to be trying to “cripple” the company and “chill public debate” over military use of AI.The Pentagon had designated Anthropic as a supply-chain risk earlier this year, marking the first publicly known instance of an American company receiving such a designation.The latest ruling does not resolve all of Anthropic’s legal disputes with the Pentagon. A separate action taken by the Defence Department under federal procurement rules remains in effect, with that matter still awaiting a final ruling.Anthropic’s AI systems had also been used by the US military in classified and sensitive operations, according to reports cited by the BBC.The legal victory comes as Anthropic prepares for a potential stock market debut, which could become one of the biggest technology listings if it goes ahead.
Article Summary: Anthropic refused to allow its AI models to be used for fully autonomous lethal weapons and mass surveillance of Americans. US District Judge Rita Lin said the government’s decision to designate Anthropic as a ‘supply chain risk’ was unlawful and violated the company's constitutional rights.

Article Title: Meet Reyha Raghavaraju, the 16-year-old Georgia student who turned her love of baking into birthday celebrations for more than 136 families in need across metro Atlanta
Article Text:
She started with what she already loved

The packages can include homemade cakes or cupcakes, gifts and handwritten birthday cards.Image credits: Saporta Report

From one celebration to 136 families

A birthday cake can seem like a small thing, a kind gesture. But for a child whose family is struggling to make ends meet, having one can mean far more than a slice of cake and a candle. Sixteen-year-old Reyha Raghavaraju saw that firsthand at a food distribution event in Georgia. She noticed a child wearing a birthday hat, but there was no birthday celebration waiting for them.The sight stayed with her. "This one kid was wearing a birthday hat," Raghavaraju said. "And then I asked him what he was doing for his birthday and he's like, 'I'm here,'" she told CBS News. The Alpharetta teenager who loved baking, began wondering if something as simple as a homemade cake could help children in families facing financial hardship feel celebrated on their special day.That question eventually became Birthday Bundles, a youth-led initiative through which Raghavaraju has helped bring birthday celebrations to more than 136 families across metro Atlanta.Reyha did not set out to build a large charitable organisation. She started with something she already knew and enjoyed doing, baking. Instead of simply donating food, she began creating birthday packages designed to make the occasion feel like a real celebration.The packages can include homemade cakes or cupcakes, gifts and handwritten birthday cards. Raghavaraju said each bundle is created with the recipient in mind, including age-appropriate gifts and a personalised message.For a child, the difference can be significant. A cake means candles to blow out. A gift means something to unwrap. A handwritten card means somebody has taken the time to think about them. Her goal was not to create elaborate birthday parties or expensive celebrations. It was to make sure that financial difficulties did not completely take away the experience of being celebrated."I think the hallmark of Birthday Bundles is what we do for every single bundle: we have a handwritten card," Raghavaraju said. "So our handwritten cards, we write them all by hand."Birthday Bundles gradually expanded. As more people learned about the teenager's work, volunteers joined her. The effort now involves around a dozen volunteers and has reached more than 136 families in the metro Atlanta area, according to CBS News Atlanta.Fourteen-year-old Saira Sharma, Raghavaraju's longtime friend and neighbour, is one of the young volunteers helping prepare the cakes and bundles. The organisation currently works with three shelter partners, including Covenant House Georgia. One recent delivery included a homemade cake and birthday bundle prepared for young people served by the organisation.Raghavaraju said the experience has changed the way she thinks about something many families may take for granted. "To me, what was shocking is that they didn't get something as simple as a birthday celebration," she said.Birthday Bundles is now looking for additional volunteer bakers, donations and shelter partners as it works to expand beyond its current North Fulton volunteer base.A homemade cake may last only a few days. A present may eventually be outgrown. A cupcake will be eaten. But the feeling of being remembered can last much longer. For a child who might otherwise have had an ordinary day, receiving a birthday package can send a simple message: your birthday matters, and so do you.
Article Summary: Sixteen-year-old Reyha Raghavaraju started Birthday Bundles to help children in families facing financial hardship. The youth-led initiative has helped bring birthday celebrations to more than 136 families across metro Atlanta. The packages can include homemade cakes or cupcakes, gifts and handwritten birthday cards.

Article Title: Indian-origin US couple on group pilgrimage to Mount Kailash goes missing after Nepal-Tibet floods
Article Text:
Deepak Ahuja, 60, and his wife Madhu Ahuja, 57.

Americans missing after Nepal floods

An Indian-origin US couple from Texas has gone missing during a pilgrimage to Mount Kailash after devastating flash floods and mudslides struck the Nepal-Tibet border, with around 90 US citizens unaccounted for, according to US officials.Deepak Ahuja, 60, and his wife Madhu Ahuja, 57, had travelled from Texas on a group pilgrimage to Mount Kailash. Their daughters, Shreya and Ashna Ahuja, told the BBC that they lost contact with their parents shortly before the floods struck and have since approached US authorities and embassies in India, Nepal and China for information about their whereabouts.The US State Department said about 90 US citizens may have been impacted by the disaster, while three Americans have been rescued. Officials said the US embassy in Nepal was working with local authorities and tour operators to assist affected Americans.The disaster also affected at least 77 people travelling with the Isha Foundation on a Kailash pilgrimage. The group was at an immigration facility near the border when the flash flood hit, according to the BBC.Initial reports suggested an earthquake may have triggered an ice avalanche and landslide.However, the US Geological Survey later said its analysis indicated that the seismic energy was generated by a landslide itself. Rainfall or melting ice may have destabilised the ground or ice, triggering the landslide and flash flooding. Scientists said it was too early to determine whether climate change contributed to the specific disaster.The Associated Press reported that about 90 Americans remained unaccounted for a day after catastrophic flash floods engulfed the Nepal-Tibet border region. The State Department said it was not aware of any US deaths and confirmed that three Americans had been rescued.Many of the missing were travelling on pilgrimages to Mount Kailash, a sacred site for Hindus, Buddhists and others.Among the missing are other Indian-origin US citizens, including 45-year-old Venus Rajnikant Patel and 72-year-old Long Island resident Jitendra Patel, AP reported.Nepal police said more than 500 tourists from 28 countries were missing, while Chinese state media reported hundreds missing in Tibet.
Article Summary: Deepak Ahuja, 60, and his wife Madhu, 57, had travelled from Texas on a group pilgrimage to Mount Kailash. Their daughters lost contact with their parents shortly before the floods struck and have since approached US authorities and embassies in India, Nepal and China for information.

Article Title: Indian-origin Miami developer Rishi Kapoor sentenced to over 11 years in $89 million fraud case
Article Text:
Rishi Kapoor/Image: Location Ventures

A Miami real estate developer of Indian origin has been jailed for 11 years and four months in prison after pleading guilty to money-laundering and payroll-tax conspiracy charges linked to an $89 million fraud scheme involving investors in his South Florida property projects, according to Miami Herald.Rishi Kapoor, 42, was sentenced on Thursday by US District Judge K. Michael Moore in federal court in Miami. Kapoor, the former CEO of Location Ventures and URBIN, told the court that he had acknowledged his “sins and crimes” and apologized to investors, former employees and his family for the harm he had caused.“I fully accept responsibility for my crimes without hesitation or excuse,” Kapoor wrote in a letter to the judge before sentencing.Kapoor was arrested in March on a 37-count federal indictment. Prosecutors said he raised at least $89 million from more than 50 investors for South Florida residential projects and owed at least $70 million in restitution to those investors. At least another $800,000 was owed to the Internal Revenue Service.The case centred on Location Ventures projects in parts of South Florida including Coconut Grove, Miami Beach, Coral Gables and Fort Lauderdale.Prosecutors alleged that money raised for individual developments was diverted for other purposes, including Kapoor's personal expenses.Kapoor pleaded guilty in May to conspiring to defraud the United States by failing to remit payroll taxes withheld from employees' wages for Social Security and Medicare between 2020 and 2022. According to the indictment, he also failed to file personal federal income-tax returns from 2019 through 2023.He also pleaded guilty to a money-laundering charge involving $820,559 transferred from his personal bank account as a down payment towards the purchase of a $5 million, 68-foot Princess yacht in 2022.The two charges to which Kapoor pleaded guilty carried a maximum combined sentence of 15 years.Prosecutors recommended that Kapoor serve 136 months in prison. His lawyers had sought a 121-month sentence, or just over 10 years, which they said was at the lower end of the applicable sentencing guidelines.Kapoor's defence also disputed prosecutors' description of the case as an $89 million fraud scheme. His lawyer Don Samuel told the court that Kapoor himself had earned about $6 million over the relevant eight-year period, including his salary from Location Ventures.“This is not a Ponzi scheme,” Samuel said. “He was not swindling anybody.”Prosecutor Elizabeth Young argued that Kapoor had raised the $89 million through “fraudulent misrepresentations” and used funds intended for one real estate project to finance another.The original federal indictment accused Kapoor of using investor money intended for real estate developments for personal expenses and other purposes. Prosecutors previously alleged that several promised condominium projects were never completed, including developments in Coconut Grove and Miami Beach.Court documents also accused Kapoor of withholding payroll taxes from employees and failing to send the money to the IRS. Prosecutors alleged that around $2 million in payroll taxes was retained rather than remitted.Kapoor was also accused of making misleading statements to banks while seeking money for the yacht and other expenses. Prosecutors said he told investors he had contributed about $13 million of his own money to the ventures, while the actual amount was roughly half that figure.The indictment further alleged that Kapoor deceived escrow agents to obtain the release of pre-construction condominium deposits and then diverted the money to personal expenses unrelated to the developments.Kapoor had built a profile in South Florida's real estate and political circles through his companies and had ties to the mayors of Miami and Coral Gables. His criminal case followed a separate Securities and Exchange Commission civil enforcement action in 2024 involving another alleged fraud scheme. Kapoor agreed to pay restitution in that matter without admitting wrongdoing.
Article Summary: Rishi Kapoor, 42, was sentenced on Thursday by US District Judge K. Michael Moore in federal court in Miami. Kapoor was arrested in March on a 37-count federal indictment. Prosecutors said he raised at least $89 million from more than 50 investors for South Florida residential projects.

Article Title: In 1992, Congress ordered the removal of 2 dams blocking the Elwha River—24 years later, the river finally ran free to the Sea
Article Text:
Image AI generated

$29.5 million plan for Elwha River dam removal

Congress protected local water supplies during Elwha River dam removal

Elwha River dam removal took decades before work began in 2011

In 1992, Congress passed an Act of law that few outside Washington State took much notice of at the time, yet it would go on to reshape one of the Pacific Northwest's great rivers. According to the Elwha River Ecosystem and Fisheries Restoration Act, the federal government was to buy up two hydroelectric dams that had blocked salmon from reaching their spawning grounds for the best part of a century, and to tear them down once and for all. They had to balance the ecological case for removal against the needs of a local paper mill, a city water supply, and the Lower Elwha Klallam Tribe, all of whom depended on the river in different ways. It took until 2011 for demolition crews to finally arrive on site. Three years later, in 2014, the job was done, and for the first time in a hundred years the Elwha ran free from the mountains to the sea.The Act did not simply order the dams torn down overnight. Instead, it set out a careful legal and financial process for the federal government to acquire the two facilities before any demolition could begin. According to Section 3 of the Act, the Secretary of the Interior was authorised "to acquire the Elwha and Glines Canyon Projects, and all rights of the owner and local industrial consumer therein, subject to the appropriation of funds therefor," but only once it had been established that dam removal was genuinely necessary for full ecological restoration.Crucially, the law fixed the price of that acquisition. As per the Act, "the consideration for acquisition of the Projects shall be $29.5 million and no more," to be paid to the dams' owner and to the local industrial consumer, the Port Angeles pulp and paper mill that depended on the power the dams produced.The Act also required the Secretary to prepare a detailed report by January 1994 examining the costs, alternatives and feasibility of removal, including, according to the Act, "the timetable after conveyance for removal of the dams and the plans for removal and disposal of sediment, debris, and other materials. "Lawmakers were careful to ensure that restoring the river would not come at the expense of the communities that had grown to rely on it. Reportedly, Section 4 of the Act required the Elwha River dam removal plan to protect local water supplies, "protection of the existing quality and availability of water from the Elwha River for municipal and industrial uses from possible adverse impacts of dam removal," with the cost of any necessary water treatment works to be borne by the federal government rather than residents.The Act also dealt with the question of power supply. Since the mill on Ediz Hook depended on electricity generated by the dams, Section 5 directed the Bonneville Power Administration to deliver so-called "project replacement power" once the dams were gone, ensuring the mill's operations would not simply collapse once the turbines stopped turning. Provision was likewise made for the Lower Elwha Klallam Tribe, with Section 7 authorising up to $4,000,000 for the purchase of land held in trust for the tribe's, as per the Act, "housing, economic development, and moorage for the Tribal commercial fishing fleet. "Turning an Act of Congress into a working demolition project took decades rather than years. Funding, environmental review and engineering preparation for removing dams of this size, the largest dam removal project in American history at the time, meant that construction crews did not begin dismantling the Glines Canyon and Elwha Dams until 2011. According to the Act, annual licences for the dams were to remain in force "until the date the Secretary has acquired title to the Projects," a condition that took many years to satisfy.The patience embedded in the 1992 law eventually paid off. By 2014, both dams had been fully removed, and the Elwha River began carrying sediment and nutrients down to the Strait of Juan de Fuca for the first time in a century. Salmon returned to stretches of river they had not reached since before the dams were built, fulfilling the ambition set out, as per the Act, at the very start: the full restoration of "the Elwha River ecosystem and native anadromous fisheries. " Twenty-four years after Congress put pen to paper, the Elwha once again flowed unbroken from the peaks of the Olympic Mountains to the sea.
Article Summary: Congress passed the Elwha River Ecosystem and Fisheries Restoration Act in 1992. It allowed the federal government to buy up two hydroelectric dams and tear them down. The dams blocked salmon from reaching their spawning grounds for the best part of a century. It took until 2011 for demolition crews to finally arrive on site. By 2014, both dams had been fully removed.

Article Title: In 1979, a Montana electrician promised to build a statue if his wife survived cancer: Six years later, a 90-foot figure stood above Butte
Article Text:
The statue is now known as Our Lady of the Rockies, and stands on the Continental Divide's East Ridge, about 3,500 feet above Butte | Wikimedia Commons

The statue is now known as Our Lady of the Rockies, and stands on the Continental Divide's East Ridge, about 3,500 feet above Butte | Wikimedia Commons

A small promise became a community project

Building a 90-foot statue on a mountain

The Continental Divide | Wikimedia Commons

A monument to mothers

Butte electrician Bob O'Bill made a promise during his wife's battle with cancer in 1979. If Joyce recovered, he would build a statue of the Virgin Mary in her honor. Joyce survived, and O'Bill eventually turned the small idea into a 90-foot statue on a mountain above Butte. The statue is now known as Our Lady of the Rockies, and stands on the Continental Divide's East Ridge, about 3,500 feet above Butte. According to the official Our Lady of the Rockies organization , construction began in 1979 and took six years, with residents contributing labor and helping raise money for the project.O'Bill's original plan was much smaller, since he had imagined a modest statue that could be placed near his home. The project grew after other people became involved. Engineers, welders, construction workers, and volunteers eventually worked on a structure far larger than the one O'Bill had first envisioned.O'Bill was an electrician who had worked for the Anaconda Company and Montana Power Co. before retiring. His wife's illness gave him the original reason for the project, but the statue soon became a community effort. The Butte-Silver Bow Public Archives records the beginning of the project in December 1979. The archives state that O'Bill promised to build a shrine if his wife recovered from cancer.Joyce did recover, and the project expanded beyond the couple into a community effort involving volunteers from around Butte. The archives state that residents spent nearly six years constructing the statue, while trying to build roads and raise money for the project.The proposed statue would stand on East Ridge, high above the city. Getting construction materials to the site required roads and other infrastructure before the statue itself could be completed. The project required a lot of funding and volunteer work. O'Bill organized fundraising while other people contributed labor, equipment and technical expertise. The statue was designed by Laurien Eugene Riehl, a retired mining engineer, and Leroy Lee, a local welder, fabricated the structure. The project did not require a commercial construction company to carry out the entire job; instead, different people contributed their skills at different stages.Butte was dealing with a difficult period in its mining history while the construction was taking place. Copper production had declined, and major changes were taking place in the local mining industry. The statue itself was constructed away from its final position, and getting it onto the mountain required another engineering operation. The official organization says workers poured a 400-ton concrete base in September 1985. The statue was ready to be transported to the East Ridge by December. It had been divided into four sections for the move.On December 17, 1985, military and civilian crews began the final operation. The Nevada Army National Guard, Montana National Guard, U.S. Army Reserve personnel from Butte and civilian workers took part in moving the sections up the mountain. The Butte-Silver Bow Public Archives records that the completed statue weighed 51 tons and was placed on the mountain in December 1985 with assistance from the Montana National Guard, Army Reserve and civilian crews. The statue was completed in December 1985, six years after O'Bill began the project. Its size was far beyond the five- to nine-foot monument originally discussed, and the finished figure ended up becoming one of the largest statues in the United States.O'Bill had originally made the promise because of his wife's illness, but the completed monument was eventually dedicated to women and mothers more broadly. The official Our Lady of the Rockies organization describes the statue as nondenominational and says it is intended as a tribute to women and mothers. A memorial wall at the site carries the names of mothers from different parts of the world. The University of Montana describes Our Lady of the Rockies as a major Butte landmark. Its account says the 90-foot statue was completed in December 1985 after being conceived by O'Bill as a tribute to the Virgin Mary following his wife's recovery from cancer. The statue now sits on private land high above the city, and can be seen from much of Butte and from surrounding roads. O'Bill died in 2016, but Joyce survived him. The original reason for the statue therefore remains part of its history, while the monument itself has taken on a wider role in Butte. The project began with a personal promise in 1979, and by December 1985, a 90-foot statue stood on the East Ridge. Its construction involved volunteers, engineers, military crews and residents who spent years raising money and preparing the site. Our Lady of the Rockies remains above Butte today, standing on the Continental Divide with the city below.
Article Summary: The statue is now known as Our Lady of the Rockies, and stands on the Continental Divide's East Ridge, about 3,500 feet above Butte. The project began in 1979 when electrician Bob O'Bill promised to build a shrine if his wife recovered from cancer. The statue was designed by Laurien Eugene Riehl, a retired mining engineer, and Leroy Lee, a local welder, fabricated the structure.

Article Title: A Missouri grandma started serving free breakfasts to neighbors in a town of fewer than 300; months later, health officials said she needed a permit to continue
Article Text:
For Kite, breakfasts were about so much more than food. She said that the people who visit her house are an extension of her family and that she didn’t want to stop providing for them.

Letter from county health officials changes things

Why a permit may be required

The department said its mission is to promote safe food-handling practices and prevent foodborne illness.

Kite says the requirements would be crushing
